source_text: CAPUT DUODECIMUM. De causis resurrectionis. Hactenus vidimus resurrectionem carnis certo futuram esse: nunc dispiciemus illius causas, nempe efficientem, materiam, formam & finem. II. Efficiens est Deus Pater, Filius & Spiritus Sanctus.
english: CHAPTER TWELVE. On the causes of the resurrection.
So far we have seen that the resurrection of the flesh is certainly future: now we shall examine its causes — namely efficient, material, formal, and final.
II. The efficient cause is God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

source_text: VI. Forma resurrectionis duplex est, interna aut externa. Interna respectu proprie resurgentium consistit in collectione cinerum, reformatione corporum, unione animarum; respectu immutandorum in subitanea immutatione qualitatum, 1 Cor. 15.51. VII. Externa consistit in ordine quo Christus in nubibus apparebit & voce sua omnes sistet ad tribunal. VIII. Finis respectu Dei est gloria Christi mediatoris; respectu hominum judicium, gloria credentium, ignominia incredulorum. Rejicimus errorem Lactantii de millenario & duplici resurrectione. Recte Gennadius: Erit resurrectio mortuorum omnium, sed una insimul & semel. Usus duplex: solatium & frenum a peccato.
english: VI. The form of the resurrection is twofold, internal or external. The internal, for those who properly rise, consists in gathering ashes, reforming bodies, uniting souls; for those to be changed, in sudden change of qualities (1 Cor. 15:51).
VII. The external consists in the order in which Christ will appear in the clouds and by his voice set all before the tribunal.

VIII. The end with respect to God is the glory of Christ the Mediator; with respect to men, the judgment, glory for believers, ignominy for unbelievers. We reject Lactantius's error of the millennium and double resurrection. Rightly Gennadius: There will be a resurrection of all the dead, but one together and at once. Double use: comfort, and a curb from sin.

source_text: De iis qui vivi offenduntur quaeri potest an sint resurrecturi, cum non ceciderint. Christus judex vivorum & mortuorum; Apostolus 1 Cor. 15.51 & 1 Thess. 4 — per demutationem mortis compendio, vivi non morituri sed mortalitate exuendi. Augustinus Retract. 2.33: Aut non morientur, aut mortem non sentient. Utraque expositio consistit. Deinde an etiam impii sint resurrecturi? Praeter recentiores Judaeos & Socinianos, opponi debent scripturae de judice vivorum & mortuorum, igne aeterno, verme qui non moritur. Resurrectio interdum stricte pro ea ad vitam beatam sumitur.
english: Of those found alive it may be asked whether they will rise, since they have not fallen. Christ is judge of living and dead; the Apostle at 1 Cor. 15:51 and 1 Thess. 4 — by a shortcut of death through change, the living will not die but be stripped of mortality. Augustine Retractations 2.33: Either they will not die, or they will not feel death. Both expositions stand. Next, will the impious also rise? Besides recent Jews and Socinians, Scripture on the judge of living and dead, eternal fire, and the worm that dies not must be opposed. Resurrection is sometimes taken strictly for that unto blessed life.

source_text: Corpus resurrecturum numero & substantia idem: 1. Matth. 10.28; 1 Cor. 15.53; Phil. 3.21; 2 Cor. 5.10. 2. ex justitia Dei (Ambrosius). 3. ab ipsa appellatione — alioquin nova creatio, non resurrectio. 4. quia mors somnus, resurrectio evigilatio. 5. ab exemplo Christi & novem particularibus exemplis. 6. a promissione immortalitatis huic carni. 7. a duplici ritu baptismi & sepulturae. Neque obstat 1 Cor. 15.50 — caro & sanguis nomine culpae arcentur. Contra Origenistarum delirium disputavit Gregorius Magnus. Subjectum quod sunt omnes qui sunt resurrecturi.
english: The body that will rise is the same in number and substance: (1) Matt. 10:28; 1 Cor. 15:53; Phil. 3:21; 2 Cor. 5:10; (2) from God's justice (Ambrose); (3) from the very name — otherwise a new creation, not resurrection; (4) because death is called sleep and resurrection awakening; (5) from Christ's example and nine particular examples; (6) from the promise of immortality to this flesh; (7) from the double rite of baptism and burial. Nor does 1 Cor. 15:50 hinder — flesh and blood are barred under the name of guilt, not substance. Against the Origenist delirium Gregory the Great disputed. The subject-quod are all who are to rise.

source_text: Resuscitatio mortuorum est opus mere divinum, longissime exsuperans omnem creaturarum virtutem, ut docet Dionysius cap. 6. de div. nominibus, ideoque immediate a Deo proficiscitur, ut praefiguratum est Ezech. 37.v.12. Pater presentat Rom. 8.v.11; 1 Cor. 6.v.14; 2 Cor. 4.v.14. Filius Joh. 5.v.28 & c.6 & 11.v.25. Spiritus Sanctus eadem vi Rom. 8.v.11. Etsi S. Trinitas communiter resurrectionis causa sit, tamen Christus est singulariter, Joh. 6.54. tum quia est causa exemplaris, tum quia potentissima vox ejus est causa instrumentalis. Si resurrectio stricte sumatur, est opus Dei immediatum; si laxius pro toto complexu ante & post, angeli resurrectionis ministri & instrumenta dici possunt, Matth. 24.v.31. Rejicimus errorem Richardi & Scoti qui putaverunt naturam resurrectionis causam esse posse.
english: The raising of the dead is a merely divine work, far surpassing every power of creatures (Dionysius On the Divine Names ch. 6), and therefore proceeds immediately from God, as prefigured in Ezek. 37:12. The Father raises (Rom. 8:11; 1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14); the Son (John 5:28; ch. 6; 11:25); the Holy Spirit with the same power (Rom. 8:11). Although the Holy Trinity is commonly the cause of the resurrection, yet Christ is specially so (John 6:54) — both as exemplar cause and because his most powerful voice is instrumental cause. If resurrection is taken strictly, it is God's immediate work; if more loosely for the whole complex before and after, angels may be called ministers and instruments (Matt. 24:31). We reject Richard and Scotus who thought nature could be a cause of the resurrection.

source_text: III. Materia resurrectionis consideratur vel ut subjectum quo, vel ut subjectum quod. Materia resurrectionis est solus homo: nam corpus illius solius, cum mortale sit, immortale redditur, ut Nemesius de nat. hominis cap. 1. Quare Mahumedus explodendus est, qui in Alcorano bestiarum resurrectionem fidei caput facit. IV. Subjectum quo est proprie caro, seu corpus hominis & quidem integrum & absolutum. Resurrectio enim proprie non fit secundum animam, sed secundum corpus: quia anima hominis est immortalis. Unde errant qui dicunt animas una cum corporibus interire, vel mori esse penitus exstingui.
english: III. The matter of the resurrection is considered either as the subject-quo or as the subject-quod. The matter is man alone: for his body alone, being mortal, is rendered immortal, as Nemesius On the Nature of Man ch. 1. Therefore Muhammad is to be exploded, who in the Qur'an makes the resurrection of beasts an article of faith.

IV. The subject-quo is properly the flesh, or the body of man, and that whole and complete. For resurrection properly is not according to the soul but according to the body, because the human soul is immortal. Hence they err who say souls perish with bodies, or that to die is to be utterly extinguished.
